title.value: Amyloid‐beta‐targeting monoclonal antibodies for people with mild cognitive impairment or mild dementia due to Alzheimer’s disease
title.quote: Amyloid‐beta‐targeting monoclonal antibodies for people with mild cognitive impairment or mild dementia due to Alzheimer’s disease

design.value: Cochrane systematic review with pairwise random‐effects meta‐analysis of randomised controlled trials, using inverse‐variance pooling, RoB 2 for risk of bias and GRADE for certainty of evidence
design.quote: We meta‐analysed results for each outcome within each comparison using the inverse variance method and the random‐effects model. We used GRADE to assess the certainty of evidence for each outcome as very low, low, moderate, or high.

phase.value: the review pooled phase‐3 randomised controlled trials
phase.quote: We found 17 eligible placebo‐controlled phase‐3 RCTs on therapy with amyloid‐beta‐targeting monoclonal antibodies in MCI or mild dementia due to AD.
phase.location: Discussion, Summary of main results, paragraph 1

n.quote: All 17 included studies were RCTs with parallel‐group randomisation. We did not find any cluster‐RCTs. The 17 studies included a total of 20,342 participants.
n.location: Results, Included studies, Study designs and settings

n_description.value: the total number of participants in the 17 randomised controlled trials included in the review (pooled participant count across included studies, not the number contributing to any single meta‐analysis)
n_description.quote: Overall, we included 17 studies with 20,342 participants. The mean age of participants in the studies ranged from 70 to 74 years.

population.value: adults with mild cognitive impairment or mild dementia due to Alzheimer's disease; seven studies enrolled only mild dementia, one only mild cognitive impairment, the rest mixed populations; mean age 70 to 74 years
population.quote: We included randomised controlled trials (RCTs) that lasted at least 12 months and compared amyloid‐beta‐targeting monoclonal antibodies with placebo or no treatment in people with mild cognitive impairment or mild dementia due to Alzheimer’s disease.

followup.value: studies lasted 18 to 27 months; results analysed at 12, 18, 24 and above 24 months, with the main analyses reported at 18 months
followup.quote: Eleven studies lasted 18 months, four lasted 24 months, and two lasted more than 24 months.

intervention.value: seven amyloid‐beta‐targeting monoclonal antibodies pooled at class level: aducanumab (3 studies), bapineuzumab (4), crenezumab (2), donanemab (1), gantenerumab (4), lecanemab (1), solanezumab (2); only the highest assessed dose was used when a trial had multiple dose arms
intervention.quote: The 17 studies assessed seven different amyloid‐beta‐targeting monoclonal antibodies: aducanumab (n = 3), bapineuzumab (n = 4), crenezumab (n = 2), donanemab (n = 1), gantenerumab (n = 4), lecanemab (n = 1), and solanezumab (n = 2).

comparator.value: placebo (all 17 included studies used placebo as the comparison)
comparator.quote: All studies compared the active medication with a placebo group.
comparator.location: Results, Included studies, Interventions and comparisons

biomarker_confirmation.value: biomarker confirmation was not an inclusion criterion of the review; individual studies varied — some required amyloid positivity by PET or CSF and others did not require it — and a sensitivity analysis was restricted to seven studies in which PET or CSF amyloid testing was abnormal
biomarker_confirmation.quote: Including only participants in whom PET or CSF testing for amyloid was abnormal: sensitivity analysis of seven studies where PET or CSF testing revealed abnormal amyloid values showed estimates consistent with those in the primary analysis for all available outcomes

limitations: Both desirable outcomes and adverse events were inconsistently reported in the studies included in the review.

Most studies did not separate people with symptoms of brain swelling and microbleeds from those in whom these effects were only visible with a scan; only four studies reported symptomatic ARIA E and only one reported symptomatic ARIA H.
The results came from studies that did not last very long; only six of the 17 studies had follow‐up longer than 18 months, which limits knowledge of longer‐term benefits and harms.

External validity is limited: mean age of trial participants was 69.5 to 73.9 years whereas mean age of onset outside the experimental setting is reported to be over 80 years, and only an estimated 5% to 15% of the AD population would be eligible for treatment.

Notable heterogeneity among studies in efficacy outcomes and in the tools used to assess them, and variation in the timing of outcome assessment, hampering precise pooled estimates and generalisability.
Some concerns about risk of bias for efficacy outcomes due to functional unblinding, which may mean the true effect size is even smaller.

All included studies were funded by the pharmaceutical industry, which in most cases controlled analysis, interpretation of data and writing of the manuscript; sponsor‐related influence cannot be excluded.
In several trials the number of participants per participating centre was low, suggesting possible selection bias; most studies included predominantly white populations in Europe and North America.
Lack of extractable data on the education level of participants, and no study reported markers of socioeconomic status.
For most undesirable outcomes the certainty of evidence was downgraded by one or two levels for imprecision.
APOE ε4 subgroup analysis was planned but not performed because most included studies did not report APOE ε4 status.
Six ongoing studies were identified and the review's conclusions may change as new results become available.
We used the methods recommended by the Cochrane Handbook and did not identify any major limitation in the review process.

risk_of_bias.judgement: some concerns for four studies, because methods of random sequence generation or allocation concealment (or both) were not described
risk_of_bias.quote: For four studies [, , , ], we evaluated the overall risk of bias as "some concerns" due to the randomisation process domain, as the methods for random sequence generation or allocation concealment (or both) were not described.

risk_of_bias.domain: measurement of the outcome — functional unblinding (efficacy outcomes)
risk_of_bias.judgement: some concerns for all studies for the efficacy outcomes, because adverse effects were much more frequent in the treated arm and could cause functional unblinding; the certainty of efficacy outcomes was downgraded one level for risk of bias
risk_of_bias.quote: for the efficacy outcomes, we judged the overall risk of bias as "some concerns" for all studies, due to bias in measurement of the outcomes, as adverse effects (i.e. infusion reaction) were much more frequent in the treated arm, which could lead to functional unblinding

risk_of_bias.domain: measurement of the outcome — safety outcomes
risk_of_bias.judgement: low risk of bias for ARIA E, ARIA H, serious adverse events and overall mortality, because MRI readers were blinded and the safety outcomes were objective
risk_of_bias.quote: We judged the safety outcomes ARIA E and ARIA H to be at low risk of bias for measurement of the outcomes, as the radiologists who read the MRIs were blind to treatment assignment in all the studies.

risk_of_bias.judgement: some concerns for three studies, which did not provide a statistical analysis plan
risk_of_bias.quote: For three studies [, , ], we evaluated the overall risk of bias as "some concerns" due to selection of the reported results, as they did not provide a statistical analysis plan.

risk_of_bias.domain: overall risk of bias by outcome
risk_of_bias.judgement: low overall risk of bias for serious adverse events and mortality; some concerns for efficacy outcomes, mainly due to functional unblinding
risk_of_bias.quote: We judged the overall risk of bias as low for the outcomes of serious adverse events and mortality. We had some concerns about the overall risk of bias for efficacy outcomes, mainly due to the risk of functional unblinding

risk_of_bias.domain: high risk of bias studies / sensitivity analysis
risk_of_bias.judgement: only one included study was at overall high risk of bias; excluding it gave pooled estimates consistent with the primary analysis
risk_of_bias.quote: Excluding studies at an overall high risk of bias: only one study had an overall high risk of bias []. Sensitivity analysis after excluding this study showed pooled estimates that were consistent with the primary analysis for all outcomes

risk_of_bias.domain: sponsor involvement / industry funding of included trials
risk_of_bias.judgement: all included trials were industry funded, with sponsors controlling analysis, interpretation and writing in most cases; sponsor‐related influence on results, particularly regarding missing ARIA data, cannot be excluded
risk_of_bias.quote: All included studies were funded by the pharmaceutical industry, which, in most cases, had control over crucial stages, such as the analysis and interpretation of data, and writing of the final manuscript.

risk_of_bias.judgement: funnel plots for the two outcomes with at least 10 studies did not suggest significant publication bias on visual inspection
risk_of_bias.quote: From our visual inspection of the plots, we did not consider them to suggest a significant risk of publication bias.

disagreements.question: Is successful removal of amyloid from the brain associated with clinically meaningful benefit in people with MCI or mild dementia due to Alzheimer's disease?
disagreements.position: The review authors conclude that successful amyloid removal does not appear to produce clinically meaningful effects, and that future research on disease‐modifying treatment should target other mechanisms of action.
disagreements.quote: Successful removal of amyloid from the brain does not seem to be associated with clinically meaningful effects in people with mild cognitive impairment or mild dementia due to Alzheimer’s disease. Future research on disease‐modifying treatments for Alzheimer’s disease should focus on other mechanisms of action.

disagreements.question: Are the observed differences on cognitive and functional scales clinically important?
disagreements.position: The review authors hold that the effects over 18 months are absent or consistently small and that the differences on ADAS‐Cog and CDR‐SB are well below the minimal clinically important difference for those scales.
disagreements.quote: The differences in the main clinical outcome measures, including ADAS‐Cog (Alzheimer's Disease Assessment Scale‐Cognitive) and CDR‐SB (Clinical Dementia Rating Scale Sum of Boxes) scores, are well below the minimal clinically important difference (MCID) on these scales.

disagreements.question: Do amyloid‐beta‐targeting monoclonal antibodies offer a favourable benefit‐to‐risk balance, as implied by the regulatory approvals of aducanumab, donanemab and lecanemab?
disagreements.position: The review authors conclude that, given small effect sizes below the MCID, the high risk of ARIA and the resource burden, these antibodies do not offer a favourable benefit to risk balance — a position the review contrasts with the approvals granted by the FDA, EMA and MHRA while noting NICE, the Dutch Health Institute and IQWiG reached negative assessments.
disagreements.quote: Given the small effect sizes, with absolute differences well below the MCID, the high risk of ARIA, and the substantial resource burden required for their administration and monitoring, monoclonal antibodies against amyloid‐beta do not offer a favourable benefit to risk balance for patients with MCI or mild dementia due to AD.

disagreements.question: Is the amyloid cascade hypothesis tenable as the main underlying mechanism of Alzheimer's disease?
disagreements.position: The review authors argue that the small‐to‐absent effects observed require the amyloid cascade hypothesis to be reconsidered as the main underlying mechanism of AD.
disagreements.quote: The small‐to‐absent effects of amyloid‐beta‐targeting monoclonal antibodies against placebo urge us to reconsider the amyloid cascade hypothesis as the main underlying mechanism of AD.

disagreements.question: Could the reported efficacy of these drugs be inflated by functional unblinding?
disagreements.position: The review authors state there are concerns that the true effect size may be even smaller than reported because common apparent adverse reactions can unblind participants and investigators, and that this bias could attenuate the difference further towards the null.
disagreements.quote: There are some concerns that the true effect size may be even smaller because of functional unblinding due to common apparent adverse reactions.

disagreements.question: Should further randomised trials of amyloid‐beta removal be conducted?
disagreements.position: The review authors judge that, given convincing evidence of the absence of a clinically meaningful effect together with the risk of cerebral oedema and microbleeds, future RCTs targeting amyloid‐beta removal are unlikely to provide clear benefit.
disagreements.quote: Given the convincing evidence of the absence of a clinically meaningful effect, in combination with a considerable risk of cerebral oedema and (micro)bleeds in the brain, from the 17 randomised controlled trials (RCTs) included in this review, it is unlikely that future RCTs targeting amyloid‐beta removal will provide clear benefit for people with AD.
